phonemes.desc: Rough breathing plus epsilon — the name opens on a rough exhale, /h/ followed by short open-mid e, like English 'heh-'.
Lambda plus acute-accented epsilon — the pitch peak falls on the penult: /lé/.
Nu plus long eta — the final syllable sustains and resolves: /nɛː/.

pronunciation.approximation: 'heh-LEH-nay' — three syllables, the high note on the middle, and the final vowel long; nothing like the two-beat English 'HEH-len.'

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Ἑλένη (Helénē), attested from Homer onward — the standard form of the name.

kin.label: Greek (folk)
kin.form: ἑλένη (helénē), 'torch' — the ancient folk-etymology linking Helen to fire and light, already noted in antiquity.

kin.label: Modern philology
kin.form: Beekes (Etymological Dictionary of Greek, s.v. Ἑλένη) judges the name probably Pre-Greek; the torch etymology is a folk-link, not science.

pronunciation.note: Helénē is Tier 1: the Greek Ἑλένη carries both the acute accent on the penult and the long eta of the final syllable — two features the ASCII 'helene' flattens. She is among the most storied mortals in the catalog: daughter of Zeús, queen of Sparta, and the woman for whom Troy burned.

domains.title: Beauty
domains.subtitle: Beauty, Sparta, Troy
domains.lead: Helénē is the daughter of Zeús whose face became the standard of beauty and the cause of the Trojan War — queen of Sparta, woman of Troy, and the most discussed mortal in Greek literature. Around her the Greeks wound every question they had about beauty, desire, blame, and whether a woman can ever be only a prize.

cards.name: Beauty
cards.desc: Iliad 3.156-158: even the Trojan elders on the wall murmur that 'no wonder' men fight for her — beauty made measurable in armies.

cards.name: Daughter of Zeús
cards.desc: Born of Zeus in the shape of a swan and Leda of Sparta; sister of the Dioscuri and of Clytemnestra, twin in blood if not in fate.

cards.name: Queen of Sparta
cards.desc: Wife of Menelaus; her palace at Sparta, with its silver bathtub and chamber of perfumes, is described in Odyssey 4.

cards.name: Helen of Troy
cards.desc: Ten years inside Priam's walls, weaving the war into cloth — the face for which a thousand ships became proverb already to Marlowe.

symbols.name: The Swan
symbols.meaning: Zeus came to Leda in the shape of a swan; beauty enters the world disguised, and the disguise is never entirely lifted.

symbols.name: Leda's Egg
symbols.meaning: Helen was hatched, not born — found in an egg beside the Eurōtas, in the account of the Catalogue of Women; beauty as something that must be broken open.

symbols.name: The Golden Apple
symbols.meaning: 'For the fairest' — the apple that made beauty contestable and therefore catastrophic; her prize and her sentence.

symbols.name: The Loom
symbols.meaning: In Troy she weaves the battles of the war into a purple web (Iliad 3.125-128): the woman's work that archives what men die for.

symbols.name: The Phantom (Eidôlon)
symbols.meaning: Stesichorus' double: 'that story is not true — you never went in the benched ships'; doubt about her guilt made into a second Helen.

symbols.name: The Tree
symbols.meaning: Helen Dendritis, 'Helen of the Tree,' received a tree-cult at Rhodes (Pausanias 3.19.10) — the goddess glimmering through the woman.

mythology.lead: Helénē's story is told by Homer, Hesiod, Stesichorus, Euripides, and Herodotus — and the tradition argues with itself at every turn: abduction or seduction, guilt or phantom, goddess or woman. She is the most examined face in Greek myth.

myths.title: Leda and the Swan
myths.text: Zeus desired Leda, the wife of King Tyndareus of Sparta, and came to her in the shape of a swan — fleeing, in the usual telling, an eagle's pursuit, so that the queen received the god under her wing. From her egg, and from a second egg, came the mixed brood of the house of Tyndareus: Helénē and her sister Clytemnestra, and the twins Kastor and Polydeukes, the Dioscuri — only some of them children of Zeus, the tradition says, though which is disputed. The earliest witness is Hesiod's Catalogue of Women (fr. 23a M-W), and Euripides opens his Helen with Leda finding the egg and hatching the child within. Aeschylus' Agamemnon (1455ff.) remembers the swan as a bird that sang for its death. The myth gives Helen a double nature from the first breath: born of a god's disguise and a mortal's bed, sister of the saviors of sailors and of the woman who would murder a king. Beauty, the story says, is never simply born — it arrives already entangled with power.

myths.title: The Oath of Tyndareus
myths.text: So renowned was Helen's beauty that suitors came to Sparta from every Greek land — and so dangerous was their number that King Tyndareus feared bloodshed whoever won. Odysseus, himself a suitor in some tellings but wise beyond courtship, proposed the oath that bears the king's name: each suitor swore to defend the marriage-rights of the chosen man, with arms if necessary. Then Helen chose Menelaus, brother of Agamemnon, and the oath bound all of Greece to her marriage. The story is preserved in Hesiod's Catalogue (fr. 198 M-W) and in the Cypria tradition; Homer has Helen on the walls of Troy look down at the Achaean champions and ask, without irony, whom they have left at home for her sake (Iliad 3.205-224). The oath converts a wedding into a treaty — and a treaty, as the next generation would learn, is only a war waiting for its pretext.

myths.title: The Apple of the Fairest
myths.text: When Paris, prince of Troy, was asked to award a golden apple inscribed 'to the fairest,' he chose Aphrodite, who promised him the most beautiful woman alive — Helen, then Menelaus' wife. What followed depends on whom you read. The Cypria tradition (Proclus' summary) makes Paris a guest in Menelaus' house who sails off with the queen while her husband is away in Crete; the Iliad says only that Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite 'came to the shepherd's valley' and that the goddess led her away (Iliad 24.25-30); Stesichorus and Herodotus insist she never went at all, carried off to Egypt while a phantom burned Troy in her shape. Homer himself refuses to settle it: Helen in the Odyssey (4.261-264) says Aphrodite 'cast in my heart sweet longing' and drove her from her marriage-bed. Abduction, seduction, or frame — the sources disagree, and the disagreement is the myth: an entire war needed a cause, and Greece could never quite decide what Helen's part had been.

myths.title: The Woman on the Walls
myths.text: Ten years in Troy, and Helénē becomes the war's most unsettled witness. In Iliad 3 she walks the wall with Priam, naming the Greek champions — Agamemnon, Odysseus, Aias, and her own brothers, whom a mist strangely prevents her from seeing. The old king, whose city is dying for her, calls her 'dear child' and refuses blame: 'for my part, I hold the gods responsible' (3.164-165). She watches Menelaus and Paris duel for her, and shudders at Aphrodite's unseen hand when the goddess spirits her stricken husband from the field. And in Iliad 6 she is found at her loom, weaving the battles of Trojans and Achaeans into a purple web — a woman archiving a war fought in her name, while Hector, gentlest of the princes, calls her 'sister' and asks only to be remembered. Homer gives Helen what later retellings often withhold: full consciousness. She is the first to blame herself — 'dog that I am' — in a poem that pointedly refuses to.

myths.title: The Phantom and Egypt
myths.text: How Helen ended the war is disputed; how she came home is, too. Stesichorus of Himera paid the price of telling her story 'wrong' — legend says he went blind — and recanted in the Palinode, preserved in Plato's Phaedrus (243a): 'that story is not true; you never went in the benched ships, nor came to the towers of Troy.' Herodotus (2.112-120), told the same by Egyptian priests, locates the real Helen in the palace of the shape-shifting sea-old man Proteus at Memphis, while a phantom went to Troy. Homer offers the peaceful third act: in Odyssey 4, Telemachus finds Helen and Menelaus at home in Sparta, magnificently reconciled, she dropping the drug nepenthe into the wine to make grief forgetful. Three endings — phantom, hostage, homecoming — and each lets her live. The tradition, unable to convict or acquit her, instead multiplied her until no single Helen could be condemned.

lore.syncretism: Behind the heroine a goddess keeps glimmering. At Therapne above the Eurōtas, Helen was worshipped beside Menelaus in a heroön — the dead honored as divine — which Isocrates (10.63) cites and Pausanias (3.15.3, 19.9) describes; Alcman already sang her as a power of Laconia. At Rhodes she was Helen Dendritis, 'Helen of the Tree,' hung in effigy, in one grim version, by the Rhodian women whose husbands she had cost (Pausanias 3.19.10). On this evidence twentieth-century scholarship proposed that a vegetation or light divinity lay behind the Homeric woman, the torch etymology her surviving trace. The Rome-ward path was quieter: Ovid stages the lovers' correspondence in Heroides 16-17, and Helen survives euhemerized as every era's emblem of fatal beauty — in Marlowe's Faustus ('Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?'), in Goethe's Faust II, where the Helena-act descends into classical Walpurgisnight, and in Rossetti's 'Helen of Troy,' who holds the apple and knows exactly what it cost.
lore.culturalLegacy: No woman of myth has been more named, blamed, or measured. 'Helen of Troy' entered every European language as shorthand for beauty that moves armies; Marlowe's 'thousand ships' made her face a unit of rhetorical currency, and to be 'a Helen' is still to be dangerously beautiful. Her name never left use — Helena, Elena, Helen remain among the most widespread given names in Christendom, from St. Helen, mother of Constantine, to innumerable Helens since. In Sparta the memory is local and warm: the Menelaion site at Therapne still carries her, and modern Greece sells 'Helen's Troy' from Mycenae to Hisarlik. Scholarship keeps re-telling her, from Homeric analysts to feminist readings that relocate the blame from Helen to the oath of the men who made her a casus belli. And the idiom endures in reverse, too — to call a conflict 'a Helen' is to admit it was fought over something not quite real.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Helénē is the West's first great argument about beauty and guilt, and the argument has never been settled because the tradition refuses the verdict. Homer gives her eloquent self-blame and then has Priam — the man with the most right to blame her — decline to. Stesichorus takes her out of Troy entirely; Herodotus hides her in Egypt; Euripides builds an entire play on the phantom so that the 'real' Helen can be innocent. Each rescue tells us less about Helen than about the culture that needed her innocent — or needed her guilty.

She is also the first fully interior woman in Western literature: on the walls, at the loom, she sees the war whole and names what she sees. Everyone else fights for her; only she describes. To restore her name with its Greek accents is to return the pitch and length of the name the elders murmured over — and to remember that the most consequential face in our literature belonged to someone allowed almost no voice of her own, and who spoke anyway.
lore.archaeology: The cult at Therapne is archaeologically secure: excavations at the Menelaion (first by the British School in 1900, decisively by H. W. Catling in the 1970s) uncovered a Mycenaean mansion beneath the Archaic-Classical shrine, with votive offerings — bronze and terracotta figurines, plaques, jewelry — addressed to Menelaus and Helen from the seventh century BCE onward, confirming the paired heroön Isocrates and Pausanias describe. The Rhodian cult of Helen Dendritis is attested textually rather than excavated. In art, Attic vase-painters of the late sixth and fifth centuries BCE made the recovery-scene a favorite: Menelaus dropping his sword at the sight of Helen among Troy's ruins (the circle of the so-called Menelaus Painter). Her 'Troy' itself — Hisarlik, excavated by Schliemann and Blegen — supplies the landscape of the legend, whatever one thinks of its historicity; the burned layers of Troy VIIa remain the war's only possible material witness.
